name: Color Channel Correlation (Gray World Variance)
description: Analyzes the statistical correlation and entanglement between the Red, Green, and Blue color channels. Authentic photography captured under natural or artificial lighting adheres to strict physical illumination laws (e.g., the Gray World assumption), creating highly entangled and predictable intra-channel relationships. Generative AI models often synthesize color by treating channels as distinct mathematical features or by applying localized stylized rendering, leading to subtle but unnatural decoupling between RGB values.
algorithm: Inter-Channel Pearson Correlation & Illumination Matrix Analysis
mechanism: The algorithm isolates the R, G, and B channels and measures their global and local statistical reliance on one another (such as R-G, R-B, and G-B Pearson correlation coefficients) within small (e.g., 32x32) blocks. Real-world scenes lit by a single dominant light source exhibit highly correlated color gradients as shadows and highlights roll off. In contrast, AI generators piece together textures from disparate training sets. This results in independent color generation where, for example, a shadow might unnaturally shift green simply because the AI lacks a unified, mathematically consistent simulated light source.
parameters: Block Resolution: 32x32 to 64x64, Metrics: Pearson correlation R-G/R-B/G-B, Global Histogram Alignment, Underlying Theory: Gray World Assumption
accuracy: Low to Moderate (60-70%) - Most effective when combined with other indicators. Its standalone accuracy is hindered by the vast variety of extreme artistic color grading techniques used by legitimate human editors.
source: Gijsenij et al. (2011) - Computational Color Constancy / Riess & Angelopoulou
useCase: Acting as an auxiliary or supplementary verification method to detect unnatural color decoupling caused by primitive AI generation or sloppy, multi-source localized photo manipulation (copy-move).

references.title: Gijsenij, A. et al. (2011). Computational Color Constancy: Survey and Experiments. IEEE TIP.
Riess, C. & Angelopoulou, E. (2010). Scene Illumination as an Indicator of Image Manipulation.

strengths:
• Extremely fast to compute, making it an excellent lightweight pass in a multi-layered forensic suite.
• Hard-coded to evaluate natural illumination properties, catching crude deepfakes that fail to simulate unified environmental lighting.
• Universally applicable across diverse image formats without needing to rely on specific compression grids (like JPEG).
limitations:
• Generally suffers from lower standalone reliability (60-70% accuracy) compared to structural or noise-based forensics.
• False positives are practically guaranteed if analyzing authentically captured photos that have been heavily stylized, cross-processed, or split-toned by professional human colorists.
• Completely useless against monochrome (black and white) imagery or minimalist vectors/illustrations.
